item.title: A Rapper’s ‘Diss Track’ Has Palestinians Asking, Who Gets to Speak for Us?
item.description:
The Palestinian rapper Shabjdeed usually makes gritty, defiant music about the struggles of living under Israeli occupation in the West Bank.

But in his latest song, “SLV," he’s turned his ire on a fellow Palestinian artist, a rising global pop star named Saint Levant. Born in Jerusalem, partly raised in Gaza, Saint Levant now lives in Los Angeles and is more likely to sing about his lovers than his homeland.

That appears to be Shabjdeed’s main gripe.

“Mixing Palestine with all kinds of bullshit and European pretentiousness, acting all chill,” Shabjdeed rapped to Saint Levant. “I’ll slap a watermelon right on your thigh — just so you know how much I love my country,” he added, a reference to the red, green and black fruit that shares the colors of the Palestinian flag.

The song, attacking Saint Levant’s persona and music as inauthentic, has drawn comparison with a similar, long-running feud between the rappers Kendrick Lamar and Drake. It has also struck a chord with many Palestinians, raising questions about their identity and representation, especially in the arts.

Palestinians have a long history of displacement, with no independent state or centralized political leadership. Who speaks for them — and how — has become a charged debate, and especially so since the Gaza war and rising Israeli settler violence in the West Bank.

Agents for Shabjdeed and Saint Levant, whose real names are Oday Abbas and Marwan Abdelhamid, did not respond to requests for comment. Both artists held competing concerts in Amman, Jordan, on Thursday night, with “SLV” included in Shabjdeed’s set.

Palestinian identity itself is complex. It has been shaped not only by a long history but also the forced expulsion and displacement of Palestinians by the creation of the state of Israel in 1948. The subsequent decades of Israeli occupation and further rounds of displacement have led to a fracturing of the Palestinian experience, with many forced to live far from their ancestral homes.

“Each of us carries a different piece of a puzzle that was shattered in 1948,” said Tamer Nafar, a rapper who is often considered the godfather of Palestinian hip-hop and co-founded the group DAM.

“The occupation dispersed us,” added Mr. Nafar, who lives in Lod, Israel. “It did not necessarily change our identity or our essence, but it certainly changed our perspective, our living conditions and the way each of us relates to Palestine.”

While the Ramallah-based Shabjdeed presents himself as the more authentically Palestinian voice, the pointed insults in “SLV” have led some to scrutinize his words and actions. Critics of the recent track accused him of not speaking out enough against the war in Gaza and noted that he continued to stage concerts during that time.

Saint Levant, 25, who often sings in Arabic as well as French and English, has made songs about Gaza and spoken out against the war during his concerts.

He has not responded to the dig from Shabjdeed, though another Palestinian rapper has.

Emsallam, a Jordanian-Palestinian musician whose real name is Msallam Hdaib, was the target of a Shabjdeed diss track in 2018. When Shabjdeed released “SLV,” Emsallam soon put out a lyrical response, urging him to rap about the war in Gaza, rather than going after other Palestinian artists.

“You don’t have any more honor — God, after this song I don’t want to hear your hisses,” Emsallam sang. “We haven’t heard your voice in three years amid all the massacres.”

Shabjdeed’s lyrics criticized Saint Levant’s focus on romance in his music, and his collaborations with Mia Khalifa, a former adult film star turned influencer and political activist, and the Lebanese pop star Haifa Wehbe.

Some Palestinians have pushed back on Shabjdeed’s criticisms, arguing in interviews and in discussions online that his lyrics feed into a long history of reducing the complexity and diversity of their lives to the political struggle.

“Palestinians are not a monolith, and we’re not all the same, and I don’t think anyone has a right to police who gets to be Palestinian,” said Tala Hammash, a fan of both artists, who runs a business in the United Arab Emirates importing pantry goods from the West Bank. “I think that’s one of the key pushbacks against the diss track against Saint Levant. So what if he talks about love and whatnot? Does that become less Palestinian?”

Ms. Hammash, who was born in Jordan and said she had not yet been able to visit her ancestral homes in Jenin and Jerusalem, added that art should grapple with every aspect of the Palestinian experience. After hearing the recent diss track, she posted a series of questions on Instagram.

“Is Shabjdeed a troll? Absolutely,” she wrote. “Are the criticisms of Marwan (SLV) valid? Yes.”

Those questions sparked discussion among her friends and followers online, and some said they felt Saint Levant performs for the tastes of Western audiences. Others said his success — from brand partnership deals to gracing the cover of fashion magazines — had come about in part because he is viewed as more Western than Arab, Ms. Hammash said.

Defenders of Saint Levant would characterize that as an unfair representation, arguing that he has put his Palestinian identity front and center. He regularly performs wearing the kaffiyeh, the black-and-white checkered scarf traditionally worn in parts of the Middle East, and waving the Palestinian flag. This summer, when he was named Prada’s new brand ambassador, he was pictured wearing a pendant depicting an outline of historical Palestine.

He has also said that his life’s goal “is to be the president of Palestine.” Saint Levant did not respond when asked, via his agent, about the criticism he had faced.

Mr. Nafar, one of the founders of Palestinian hip-hop, said that while he felt Saint Levant’s music was coming from a good place, his representation can feel simplistic, trendy and disconnected from the complex reality that Palestinians on the ground live every day.

Rather than shrink from the controversy, though, he encouraged Saint Levant to clap back and engage in a discourse that wrestles with questions of place, authenticity and who gets to tell which story, issues inherent to hip-hop, he said.

“As a rapper I say, ‘Yalla Saint,’” Mr. Nafar said, using the Arabic word for “let’s go.”

“Get your diss track back, and let the story go on,” he added.

Heedo Abu Laban contributed reporting.

item.title: Britain’s Farage Takes a Page From Trump’s Playbook Amid Investigations
item.description:
Nigel Farage, Britain’s leading right-wing politician, faced a dilemma last month.

What do you do when the inquiries and accusations are piling up? The police are looking into one of your donors. You are being investigated for potentially breaking Parliament’s rules because you didn’t report a £5 million gift. The news media are publishing new allegations almost daily.

For Mr. Farage, the leader of the Reform U.K. party, the answer appears to have been clear: Attack your critics, undermine the regulatory or judicial processes by labeling them illegitimate before they conclude, and seek pre-emptive absolution from “the people” — your most loyal supporters.

He was borrowing a page from a playbook honed over the years by other embattled populists like President Trump, Marine Le Pen, the French far-right leader, and Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister. Mr. Farage resigned his parliamentary seat and immediately ran for it again in the resulting special election.

On Friday, he declared himself completely vindicated by his victory in the contest in Clacton, in eastern England.

“I wanted the people of Clacton, the voters of this constituency, to be my judge,” he said in an early-morning victory speech while votes were still being counted. “Not the mainstream media in Britain and the political establishment who paint us out to be criminals and bad people every day. I asked the voters of Clacton to be my jury, and the verdict has now come in.”

The result was hardly surprising. Mr. Farage won in a safe Reform U.K. seat, collecting 63 percent of the vote in an election that all the other major parties boycotted and called a stunt. His main challenger? A novelty candidate called Count Binface, who wears a trash can over his head.

The question now is whether the gambit will work, or whether British voters outside of his party’s core base will continue to pay attention to the questions swirling around Mr. Farage about donations and expensive gifts. In the weeks since revelations about his undisclosed benefits were first published in The Guardian and The Sunday Times, his personal poll ratings have fallen, and Reform’s position in national polls has slipped.

Within hours of his speech on Friday, the office of the parliamentary standards commissioner restarted its investigation into Mr. Farage’s failure to declare the 5 million pound gift (about $6.7 million) from a British crypto-billionaire based in Thailand. (Mr. Farage has said he didn’t need to register it because it was a personal gift given before he was a member of Parliament.)

Yet Mr. Farage has proved to be a resilient political survivor who successfully tapped into public anger about successive British governments. His decades-long campaign to limit immigration remains one of the most potent issues in the country, and Reform is still polling within the margin of error of the governing Labour Party and above the Conservatives.

And he is not wrong to notice that the go-on-the-offense political strategy has worked well for several of his peers across the world who, like him, have denied any wrongdoing.

Take Mr. Trump. After leaving office in 2021, he faced a battery of criminal charges and civil lawsuits for accusations including falsifying business records, illegally retaining documents containing national security secrets, trying to reverse the results of the 2020 election, and sexual abuse and defamation.

Mr. Trump railed about the “witch hunts” being conducted by the “establishment” and accused the news media of being the “enemy of the people.” He said judges, prosecutors, F.B.I. agents, intelligence officers and election officials were all corrupt or incompetent — or both.

But most of all, he insisted that none of it would matter to the American voters.

“Your victory will be our ultimate vindication, your liberty will be our ultimate reward and the unprecedented success of the United States of America will be my ultimate and absolute revenge,” Mr. Trump said on the campaign trail in 2024.

By November 2024, when more than 77 million people chose to return Mr. Trump to office, most of the criminal and civil charges against him had either stalled, been dismissed or been nullified by the Supreme Court.

Tony Travers, a professor of politics at the London School of Economics, said Mr. Farage and his allies are betting that he can convince the British public to see the Reform leader in the same way that many Americans see the president — as a victim of unfair persecution.

“That is pretty similar to Donald Trump, it seems to me,” Mr. Travers said. “That people are prepared to overlook all the cryptocurrency stuff and the self-enrichment that’s going on, because somehow he’s different, he’s an outsider.”

In France, Ms. Le Pen was found guilty last year of embezzlement by a criminal court and barred from running for public office for five years. She called the ruling a “political” attempt to thwart her.

“I’m not going to submit to a democratic denial so easily,” Ms. Le Pen added.

When the five-year ban on running for office was lifted by an appeals court last month, she immediately declared: “This evening, I am a candidate in the presidential election.” Like Mr. Trump, she is betting that voters in a national election will look past her legal troubles.

On Friday, Jordan Bardella, a protégé of Ms. Le Pen and the president of their National Rally Party, congratulated Mr. Farage on his victory, writing on social media: “Nigel Farage had the courage and dignity to submit himself once again to the judgment of the voters, the sole masters in a democracy.”

Mr. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader, has used similar political tactics to try to undermine bribery and corruption charges that were leveled against him years ago.

He was indicted in 2019 on charges of giving or offering lucrative favors to several media tycoons in exchange for favorable news coverage or gifts worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. He appropriated one of Mr. Trump’s favorite phrases, calling the corruption investigations a “witch hunt,” as well as “a joke” and “an absurdity.”

But in 2022 he was re-elected as prime minister in what he characterized as a total rejection of the charges against him.

“We have won a huge vote of confidence from the people of Israel,” he said.

It remains to be seen whether Mr. Farage’s attempt to appeal to “the people” over the outcome of the investigations will succeed in Britain.

His by-election victory on Thursday was in a tiny, Reform-friendly corner of the country, hardly a nationwide referendum on his actions. And, as a general election does not have to be held until 2029, it may be some time before we find out.

item.title: In Barcelona, Finding the Perfect Spot for Vermut and Snacks
item.description:
Spaniards really like their bars.

There are probably more bars in Spain per capita than any other European country, roughly one bar for every 175 people, according to a recent count.

And maybe no city in Spain reveres its bars as much as Barcelona. They are historical, cultural and usually, personal. Imagine Spanish “Cheers” and you start to get an idea. But in recent years, many of these establishments, known as bodegas — the kind populated by locals, with wooden casks of wine and vermut on tap — had been dying off.

The culprit?

“In two words: rents and greed,” said Ricard Martin, the food and drink editor for Time Out Barcelona. When rental laws were loosened around 2014, he said, landlords hiked rents that had long been regulated. Many bodega owners couldn’t afford them, sold off their licenses and retired. The places that opened in their wake weren’t aimed at inhabitants, but at tourists.

But as concerns about overtourism grew across the country, locals pushed back. In 2014, two local businessmen, Lito Baldovinos and Enric Rebodosa, bought one of Barcelona’s most forgotten bars, La Confiteria, to revive it. It worked: In 2015 the City Council designated the bar an “emblematic establishment,” which marks it as a business worthy of protection. To date, their company, Grupo Confiteria, has saved 15 establishments.

“What makes these bars unique is that they’re not designed as concepts. They’re the result of time,” Mr. Baldovinos said. “Layers of history, architecture, habits and people accumulate naturally.”

If you know where to look across the city, the bodegas are still there. Each bears their neighborhood’s fingerprint, but also shares a common trait: They look like they were decorated from a yard sale. Maybe there’s a trumpet on a shelf, or a painting of someone’s dead grandmother. Perhaps a framed picture of a sports team, or a black-and-white photo from a century earlier when everyone wore hats.

During a recent two-week stay, I wandered Barcelona in search of bodegas. This list isn’t definitive — think of it as a snapshot of neighborhood bars romantically stuck in the Barcelona of decades, maybe centuries, past.

On my first day out, jackpot: Bar Gelida in the middle of the Eixample neighborhood. Even in the early afternoon the bar was lousy with locals three deep. Its tiled walls and tall ceilings had a way of amplifying the conversation and the fluorescent, unflattering lighting. Gelida sits on the corner — which isn’t the usual 90-degree corner of most city blocks. In Eixample each street corner is cut at a 45-degree angle, or “chamfered,” creating octagonal intersections. The result is more sidewalk real estate to grab a table, order a plate of tripe stew and smoke.

Carrer de la Diputació, 133

Bar Bodega Gol, in the San Antoni neighborhood, is what you would get if you crossed a 75-year-old Catalonian bar with a loud, passionate soccer club. A handful of men were outside wearing Adidas track suits, smoking cigarettes and debating a match. Inside, the walls were lined with framed pictures of players, jerseys, trophies, pennants, soccer balls — everything but the pitch. Pity the person in an AC Milan jersey.

Every table was packed with glasses of beer and plates of pintxos: patatas bravas, calamari in olive oil, peppers, anchovies speared with a toothpick. (Bars, unlike restaurants, serve pintxos at room temperature.) People were speaking Catalan and Spanish, and laughing, eating, debating, arguing. Just not a word of English.

Carrer del Parlament, 10

El Pollo’s windows are perfectly positioned to take in businessmen, students and professionals walking outside, meeting up with friends at sidewalk cafes or jumping on their Vespas. I ordered a piece of Spanish tortilla, a glass of Verdejo and sat down to voyeur away an afternoon with my friend Kiki in the neighborhood of El Raval.

“We’re old fashioned in Barcelona. We believe that meeting people in real life is important,” said the owner Aimar Cordoba Bilbao. He has owned El Pollo for five years, but his ethos is loyal to a much older past. “It’s my grandmother’s recipe,” he said, pointing to the tortillas.

Carrer del Tigre, 31

Small and dimly lit, Bar Bodega Marin in the Gracia neighborhood has walls lined with wine bottles, casks and cases. Luis Sologuren, a Venezuelan man who bought the bar with his wife, Vanessa, in 2022, told me that since 1896 there have only been four owners. “In the old days, the usual customer was maybe 80 or 90 years old, and he would order one beer and sit on the same stool for three hours. It was not sustainable.”

Mr. Sologuren now serves food and sells wine, but a few old-timers still enjoy sitting on the same stool for the better part of the afternoon.

Carrer de Milà i Fontanals, 72

Technically, Bianco Noir, in El Raval, was opened by an Italian man and his French wife. But the décor, the lighting and the vibe are thoroughly of Barcelona. An ancient stone wall on one side, shelves of wine and liquor on the other, Bianco Noir feels like it hasn’t changed in a century.

The bar serves pintxos as well as larger meals like lentil stew, even bowls of pasta. “We don’t work to get rich,” said Christian Torlone, an owner, referring to bodega owners. “We don’t serve paella and sangria, the tourist menu.”

“I wanted to open a bar where people have a nice chat, enjoy a glass of wine, maybe watch a Barce game,” he added. “The bodegas of the 21st century have no soul. I wanted a place with a soul.”

Carrer de la Riera Alta, 8

Standing room only, line out the door, an array of food limited only by your imagination: This is the phenomenon of Quimet Y Quimet in the neighborhood of El Poble-sec.

When it opened in 1914, the bar only sold its own vintage but as the neighborhood grew, so did the bar’s offerings — eventually including a huge selection of wine, vermut and food. Shrimp with roasted red peppers, leeks with caviar, beans with cod, salted tuna with artichokes, anchovies with olives, some things glistening in olive oil, others dripping in honey, jamon in every form.

What didn’t change was the owner: Quimet Y Quimet has been in the same family for over a century.

Carrer del Poeta Cabanyes, 25

Follow New York Times Travel on Instagram and sign up for our Travel Dispatch newsletter to get expert tips on traveling smarter and inspiration for your next vacation. Dreaming up a future getaway or just armchair traveling? Check out our 52 Places to Go in 2026.

]]>

item.title: How Cyclospora Evaded the U.S. Food Safety System to Sicken Thousands
item.description:
Cases of cyclosporiasis were mounting rapidly in Michigan and state health officials were homing in on a common thread: Many of those who had fallen ill had eaten at Taco Bell.

On July 1, they asked the company for its supply chain records, crucial information in tracing ingredients that may have caused the outbreak.

On July 3, they wrote and asked for the records again.

On July 6, they wrote a third time.

“With the rapid nature of this outbreak and the number of people affected, we need to ensure we are completing traceback in a timely manner to preserve public health,” Lauren Edwards, an epidemiologist on the state’s rapid response team, said in an email to executives at Yum Brands, which owns Taco Bell. (The New York Times obtained the correspondence under Michigan’s open records law.)

Later that day, Taco Bell provided some records to the state, which by then was working with the federal Food and Drug Administration. The F.D.A. asked for additional records two days later. Finally, on July 13, the agency received all the records it needed to pinpoint lettuce from a Taylor Farms plant in Mexico as a source of the outbreak.

A federal rule that had been scheduled to take effect in January would have required Taco Bell to send those records within 24 hours. But last year, the Trump administration delayed the implementation of that rule until mid 2028, saying companies needed more time to prepare.

Food safety experts say the postponement has hindered the response to the outbreak, the largest cluster in a record number of cyclospora cases in the United States this year.

“Time translates into illnesses and lives,” said Thomas Gremillion, director of food policy at the Consumer Federation of America, who reviewed the emails from Michigan. He added: “We would have had a much better response to this outbreak if they hadn’t delayed that rule.”

Cyclospora, which can cause explosive diarrhea, cramps and other severe symptoms, has been a recognized driver of foodborne illness for nearly 30 years. But this year’s massive toll — totaling more than 24,500 confirmed or suspected cases so far and two deaths — reveals shortcomings in the U.S. food safety system that may leave Americans more vulnerable to future pathogens, public health experts say.

Many point to an erosion of food safety oversight during the Trump administration, stemming in part from its aggressive efforts to roll back regulations and shrink the federal government. Last year, the F.D.A. laid off many of the staff who supported food inspectors’ travel planning and who coordinate with foreign governments on food safety. (An F.D.A. spokesman said on Friday that “travel support staff and staff that coordinated with foreign governments have been reinstated.”) The administration eliminated a committee tasked with studying problems that led to outbreaks. It also cut a program focused on cyclospora tracking.

“So far this administration has made our food less safe, not safer,” said Scott Faber, the senior vice president for government affairs at the Environmental Working Group. “By firing food safety experts, by reducing the number of inspections, by tracking fewer pathogens, and by failing to set up a traceability system that makes sure that we’re able to to clear the shelves quickly.”

Donald Prater, the F.D.A.’s acting deputy commissioner for food, said the agency responded swiftly with the information it had on hand. He added that even if the 24-hour rule had been in effect, it would not have made a major impact on managing this outbreak response.

An F.D.A. spokesman said that protecting the nation’s food supply remains a core responsibility, and the agency has the personnel and resources to respond to outbreaks of foodborne illnesses.

Taco Bell said it responded to requests from Michigan and federal officials in a timely manner. “We acted immediately, voluntarily and proactively to protect our guests and support health officials,” the company said in a statement.

On July 15, federal authorities tied the outbreak to iceberg lettuce that had been supplied to Taco Bell from a plant in Mexico owned by Taylor Farms, the large U.S.-based producer of fresh vegetables, fruits and greens. The next day, Taylor Farms began a recall of their products containing iceberg lettuce that had been shipped to 27 states.

A spokeswoman for Taylor Farms said it promptly responded to requests for information and is cooperating with health officials in the U.S. and Mexico. On July 19, it sent independent third-party experts to conduct a “top-to-bottom review” of food safety processes there.

Yet efforts by authorities to figure out how the iceberg lettuce in Mexico became contaminated by cyclospora, a single-cell parasite that infects the small intestine and spreads through feces, continue to move slowly. Although Taylor Farms temporarily shut down the plant on July 18, F.D.A. inspectors did not arrive in Mexico to inspect it until this week, nearly a month later.

The investigators from the F.D.A. were delayed in traveling partly because of clearances needed to work in an area deemed unsafe for Americans, according to a person familiar with the effort, who was not authorized to speak about it. They also needed to coordinate with the Mexican government and gather enough testing supplies to do a thorough investigation, the person said.

The slow start could make it difficult to discover a root cause of the contamination, said Sandra Eskin, chief executive of Stop Foodborne Illness, a nonprofit working to protect against foodborne pathogens.

Some of the problems that have hampered the response to this outbreak developed over decades: Scientists who study cyclospora said they have lacked the funding to better understand the parasite, including how it spreads and how to detect it. Food safety advocates say the goals of a landmark food safety law enacted in 2011 have not been met amid weak regulations and falling numbers of foreign food facility inspections.

The federal rule requiring companies to swiftly produce records in an outbreak investigation was drafted under that law, the Food Safety Modernization Act, which gave the F.D.A. new powers to keep food free of parasites and pathogens, to rapidly trace produce through the supply chain and to aggressively expand inspections.

The law set a goal of 19,200 annual foreign inspections by 2016. But foreign inspections have fallen markedly even as the foreign food supply has surged. In 2025, the agency made about 1,100 visits to foreign food plants and cited significant lapses in about 80 of them. Its last visit to the Taylor Farms facility in Mexico was in 2019, records show.

Even though finding the tiny cyclospora parasites during a site visit is challenging, such visits could reveal indicators such as irrigation water with high levels of fecal matter.

A spokeswoman for Taylor Farms said that it has a “robust fecal indicator testing program that includes cyclospora for all of our water sources. All of those tests have been negative.”

With the exception of the pandemic years, the F.D.A.’s foreign food inspections in 2025 were at a 15-year low, agency data show.

Currently, the F.D.A. has about 440 staff charged with inspecting more than 300,000 registered animal and human food facilities — domestically and abroad.

“Other things help ensure the safety of the food supply, but inspection is the classic consumer protection when it’s done correctly,” Ms. Eskin said.

Another major safeguard outlined in the law was meant to add visibility into the food supply chain, particularly for public health officials and regulators charged with limiting harm during an outbreak.

The rule that the F.D.A. ended up delaying last year was meant to “limit food-borne illness and death.” It required food sellers, including restaurants and grocers, to provide the agency or an authorized representative with a spreadsheet detailing their suppliers within 24 hours of an outbreak, or a reasonable amount of time the agency agrees to.

The F.D.A.’s decision to delay the rule was followed by action from the Republican-controlled Congress, which took additional steps to bar the F.D.A. from using its funding to enforce the rule and urged a revision favoring greater flexibility.

In Michigan cyclospora has now sickened more than 12,000 people and contributed to two deaths. Officials said in the internal emails, which were first obtained by Bloomberg News, that they had to contend with an antiquated disease surveillance system and analyze the information from interviews with 700 people who fell ill.

Once Taco Bell emerged as a common thread the interviews, getting the company’s supplier list was crucial, said Susan Mayne, a former F.D.A. official who remains active in food policy. In such a large outbreak, she said, it’s important to determine if one ingredient came from a central source, in contrast to those from an array of farms.

“The faster you can get back to the records, the faster you can identify the source of the outbreak and remove those products from the market and prevent further exposures,” she said. “So speed is everything.”

This week is not the first time F.D.A. officials flew to Taylor Farms’ Mexican processing plant to investigate a cyclospora outbreak.

In 2013, in the wake of an outbreak that sickened more than 600 people who ate salad at Olive Garden and Red Lobster, federal inspectors descended on the facility and examined more than 1,000 samples of lettuce, irrigation water and the feces of the farm workers, a main harbor for the cyclospora parasite.

They found virtually nothing, an inspection report shows. Every result was negative, except for one considered inconclusive.

The F.D.A. did note that the facility’s practice of washing the salad mix with recycled water had the potential to spread cyclospora, if it was present. But ultimately the agency could not “determine how or at what point in the supply chain” the cyclospora was introduced. Taylor Farms said it then began a new process for testing water and produce.

Jim Gorny, a produce safety expert who retired in 2024 from the F.D.A., said cyclospora wasn’t viewed inside the agency as high-risk like E. coli or listeria. Yet, some scientists were growing increasingly worried as cyclospora outbreaks grew in size and scope. Originally found in berries and basil, by the 2000s, it was affecting larger numbers of people after eating salad.

Cyclospora is a uniquely difficult parasite to detect, monitor and eliminate. Testing for it in the environment — especially in agricultural water — is extraordinarily challenging, and, as a result, rarely done.

Moreover, cyclospora does not grow in laboratory culture. Scientists often use culture as a tool to amplify tiny bits of bacteria, like salmonella or E. coli, to detectable levels. The same cannot be done for cyclospora, said Kalmia Kniel, a microbiologist at the University of Delaware who researches the parasite.

And because cyclospora are distributed sparsely in large volumes of water, finding them is like dipping a net in the ocean to find a single type of fish. There’s also no way to kill them in processing plants that wash produce like lettuce: They can survive chlorination, a standard process used to kill bacteria.

Dr. Kniel and other food safety researchers have been asking the government repeatedly for $10 million to fund work to develop new ways to spot the cyclospora in the environment and to set testing standards. But after four consecutive years submitting grant proposals to the United States Department of Agriculture, the work remains unfunded.

The U.S.D.A. said its peer reviewers had selected projects viewed as “most impactful” for growers and that it had supported some cyclospora research last year.

Dr. Gorny noted that he helped develop an F.D.A. action plan for cyclospora that was released in 2023. The plan called for increased and improved education, testing for cyclospora and rapid root-cause analysis of outbreaks. Recently, officials working on the plan held an educational session in a region of Mexico that had been tied to prior cyclospora outbreaks.

But progress toward solutions has been slow. F.D.A. guidance on produce safety released this week acknowledged that the agency does not know of any treatment the would prevent the spread of cyclospora “and be suitable for use on fresh-cut produce.”

As a result, there may be more summers of cyclospora.

“Until we get down to the hard work of better research, getting tools for better and faster detection and better root cause analysis,” Dr. Gorny said, “this is going to happen again.”

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi contributed reporting.

item.title: Israeli Strikes in Lebanon Kill 11, Health Officials Say
item.description:
A pair of Israeli strikes killed at least 11 people in southern Lebanon early Saturday, the Lebanese health ministry said, one of the deadliest attacks in the country since a fragile truce took effect nearly two months ago.

A strike overnight in Ansar, near the city of Nabatieh, killed seven people, including three children, and wounded two others, health ministry officials said. Hours later, Israeli warplanes carried out an airstrike on Deir al-Zahrani, killing at least four and wounding 17 others, according to the ministry.

The Israeli military said in a statement that its attacks in the Ansar area had targeted infrastructure belonging to Hezbollah, the Iran-backed militant group. It did not respond to a request for comment on the reports of civilian deaths or on the attack later on Saturday morning.

Nawaf Salam, Lebanon’s prime minister, called the escalation on Saturday “extremely dangerous” and said it undermined efforts to establish stability in the country’s south.

“The seven martyrs in the Israeli strike on Ansar town were not ‘military infrastructure,’ and the children and women killed were not military targets,” Mr. Nawaf said on social media.

The office of Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said later on Saturday that Hezbollah had attacked Israeli soldiers inside Lebanon, seriously injuring three of them. The military, it said in a statement, then struck the group’s “headquarters which ordered the attack” and only later learned “that Hezbollah deliberately put civilians in that military compound.”

When approached for comment, a Hezbollah spokesman denied that claim. The group condemned the attacks in a separate statement, accusing Mr. Netanyahu of escalating the war “in order to strengthen his domestic political position.” The group vowed that the strikes would be “met with an appropriate response.”

A cease-fire reached in mid-June was meant to halt the fighting between Israel and Hezbollah and pave the way for establishing a more durable peace. But the truce has since frayed, with fighting between the two sides continuing across southern Lebanon.

The strikes on Saturday come as Israel and Lebanon remain at odds over the terms of a “framework agreement” that was intended to wind down the conflict after months of U.S.-mediated negotiations in Washington and Rome.

Under the agreement, signed on June 26, Israel is expected to gradually withdraw from territory it occupies in southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese Armed Forces would then deploy in those areas and help facilitate the return of residents displaced by the fighting.

The framework has been criticized in Lebanon because it does not set out a timetable for the Israeli withdrawal, and because it links the process to the Lebanese government’s efforts to disarm Hezbollah, which the state has long struggled to do.

Hezbollah itself was not a party to the U.S.-brokered negotiations and has rejected direct talks with Israel.

In a statement published online by his office on Saturday, Lebanon’s president, Joseph Aoun, condemned “Israel’s repeated violations of the framework agreement” along with the “international laws requiring the protection of civilians.”

The war in Lebanon began in early March after Hezbollah fired into Israel in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. The subsequent fighting has killed more than 4,300 people and wounded more than 12,000, according to Lebanon’s health ministry. More than one million people have been displaced as Lebanon’s economic and humanitarian crises have deepened, according to the International Organization for Migration.

Israel has continued to occupy swaths of southern Lebanon. In recent weeks, it has demolished buildings in areas it controls and carried out sporadic attacks in the south, including airstrikes and drone strikes, according to Lebanese officials and state media. The Israeli military says the operations aim to dismantle Hezbollah infrastructure and prevent the group from rearming and threatening northern Israel.

As part of their attack early Saturday, Israeli forces blew up buildings in the southern town of Bint Jbeil and several nearby villages, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported.

Israel marks the boundary of the area it controls on its maps, and says that it considers any armed person operating south of that demarcation line as a security threat and a legitimate military target.

In a televised speech on Friday, Hezbollah’s leader, Naim Qassem, condemned the recent Israeli strikes, saying they demonstrated the futility of negotiating with Israel. He also criticized the pace and manner of the Israeli withdrawal, and the difficulties faced by the Lebanese Army in taking control of those areas and enabling displaced residents to return.

“These negotiations will bring nothing but shame and disgrace,” Mr. Qassem said.

Hwaida Saad, Aaron Boxerman and Sarah Chaayto contributed reporting.

item.title: Iran Says Qatar Captured Three of Its Pilots Early in War With U.S.
item.description:
Iran has accused Qatar of capturing three of its bomber pilots in the early days of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, and on Saturday called on the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene on their behalf.

Gen. Seyed Mohammad Bagherzadeh, commander of the Iranian armed forces’ missing persons search committee, wrote to the global aid organization in a letter published by Iranian media. He said the men were flying Su-24 fighter jets in an operation on March 2, days after the outbreak of the war, when their planes had been hit by “enemy defenses” and the pilots ejected.

They survived but were captured by the Qatari authorities, according to General Bagherzadeh, who named the men as Javad Salehi, Abdolmajid Dashtian and Omran Behraveshian. A fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, died, he added.

The Red Cross and a Qatari government spokesman did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

General Bagherzadeh’s letter was the most precise indication so far of what Iran believes happened to the three pilots. Before Saturday’s letter, Iranian authorities had said the fate of the men was unknown.

Qatar, a close U.S. ally that hosts a major American military base, said on March 2 that its Air Force had shot down two Iranian Su-24 bomber jets. Iran lashed out at its Persian Gulf neighbors soon after it was attacked by the United States and Israel.

Qatar “has not allowed the prisoners to meet or speak with their families or with officials handling their cases,” General Bagherzadeh wrote. He called on the Red Cross to meet with the pilots, investigate their condition, and facilitate their release as soon as possible.

Aaron Boxerman contributed reporting.

item.title: $10 Million in Gold Found Buried Under Former Brewery in Belgium
item.description:
When the police chief learned what workers had found, sealed inside a small brick cellar as they drilled below a defunct brewery, he was sure someone had interrupted his Tuesday meeting with a prank.

“I thought it was a joke,” said the chief, Patrick Feys, “because things like that normally don’t happen in real life.”

But the workers had plenty of proof: 49 gold bars and more than 4,000 gleaming coins, a cache worth an estimated $10 million, its origin and fate unknown.

Construction workers in the Belgian city of Dendermonde had been drilling this week beneath what used to be the foundation of a brewery built in the 1890s. The site was undergoing renovations for a project to create transitional housing for homeless people. At first, the workers thought they had only found one-euro coins, and kept boring through the cellar’s brick walls, Chief Feys said.

Instead, they started finding gold bars — leaving dents and scratches on a few with their tools.

After the discovery, Chief Feys’s mounting excitement merged with anxiety, he said. The police hurried the trove to the station for inventory, where four people counted each piece under a surveillance camera to ensure nothing was lost or stolen.

“An amount like this, it’s always a risk,” Chief Feys said, adding that he did not relax that day until the stash was in federal custody.

Geert Hillaert, the director of the social services nonprofit that owns the property where the gold was found, said in an interview that two questions sprang to mind when he heard about the buried treasure: “How does this happen?” and “How do we get it safe?”

But after police took custody of the gold, a third question arose: Who will get to keep it?

Local prosecutors will investigate whether the gold has been stolen or involved in any crime, Mr. Hillaert said. If not, Belgian law gives family members or other heirs five years to claim the bounty, he and the police said.

But there do not appear to be any direct, living heirs of the brewery’s original owner, whom former mayor Piet Buyse has identified as a man named Théophile van Assche. In an interview with the Dutch-language Belgian outlet HLN, Mr. Buyse said the brewery was built in the late 19th century, and Mr. van Assche’s three children ran the business until it shuttered in 1970.

None of the children married or left heirs, Mr. Buyse said, and there are few ready clues as to the origin of the gold. The authorities said a stamp on one of the gold bars dated it to the 1960s.

In 1982, the property was left to a local Benedictine monastery, which used it as transitional housing for formerly incarcerated people, Mr. Hillaert said. Last year, the monks gave the property to CAW Oost-Vlaanderen, the nonprofit that Mr. Hillaert directs. (The monastery did not respond to a request for comment.)

If the gold eventually goes to his nonprofit, Mr. Hillaert said he hoped to use the money to build more housing for families without homes. His government-funded nonprofit also provides services for victims of abuse, young people, immigrants and formerly incarcerated people.

Chief Feys said at least three people had already come to the police saying they had ties to the unearthed family fortune. While investigators worked to ensure the gold was not connected to any crime, Chief Feys said he recommended the people claiming the riches find legal help.

Mr. Hillaert said he would consult with the nonprofit’s lawyers, but that he did not think the group would contest a legal claim if a family member or other legitimate recipient came forward.

“We are not that sort of an organization,” he said.

item.title: Canadian Petition to Expel U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra Takes Off
item.description:
After boycotting American products and shunning vacations south of the border, Canadians in their thousands are pouring their incandescent anger at the United States into a new cause: ousting the American ambassador.

More than 160,000 people have signed a petition to the Canadian Parliament, submitted by a Calgary resident on July 21, calling for the removal of the ambassador, Pete Hoekstra.

The petition asserts that Mr. Hoekstra, a faithful messenger of President Trump’s aggressive stance toward Canada, has harmed U.S.-Canada relations. The two countries are locked in a trade war, and their relationship, once the closest two nations can be, has been at a historic low since Mr. Trump retook office.

Just 500 signatures are legally required to bring an online petition to the Parliament floor for discussion, and this one will most likely be put forward for debate in the fall by Elizabeth May, the leader of Canada’s Green Party.

The petition lays out the reasoning for Mr. Hoekstra’s removal: it argues that he has “normalized the Trump administration’s threats to annex Canada as the 51st state.” Mr. Hoekstra has reposted Mr. Trump’s 51st-state jabs on social media and has dismissed Canadians’ anger at the rhetoric as “emotional” and inexplicable.

It also states that Mr. Hoekstra has interfered in Canadian politics in a manner “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol.” It lays out how activists from Alberta seeking to break away from the rest of the country repeatedly met with State Department officials, “raising serious questions about U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian unity.”

The petition calls on the Canadian government to invoke the Vienna Convention of Diplomatic Relations, the international accord that governs diplomacy, declare Mr. Hoekstra “persona non grata” and request his removal from office, as well as to set up a parliamentary committee to review “U.S. diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs."

The United States Embassy in Ottawa referred questions to the State Department, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The petition culminates months of souring public sentiment toward Mr. Hoekstra personally, mirroring the plummeting views toward the United States generally.

Polling shows Canadians’ opinion of the United States has rapidly gotten worse since Mr. Trump took office and began targeting Canada with tariffs and talk of making it part of the United States. A Pew survey published in June found that only 35 percent of Canadians now view the United States as a reliable partner, down sharply from 2022, when it was 82 percent. Canadian recreational visits to the United States have shrunk by more than a quarter over the past year.

In this context, Mr. Hoekstra, a former Republican Representative from Michigan, has become notorious in Canada for his blunt, unapologetic tone, which channels Mr. Trump’s.

One comment that drew ire came in November, when Mr. Hoekstra was asked if he understood why Canadians found Mr. Trump’s 51st state remarks upsetting.

“Here, I’ll just get myself in trouble,” he said. “I go around the country and people will say, ‘Pete, you just don’t understand why we’re so mad about the 51st state.’ Yeah, you’re right. I don’t.”

Unlike some of his colleagues, Mr. Hoekstra has never been summoned by the Canadian government, a step taken when a diplomatic emissary is seen as overstepping so badly that the host government needs to give them a talking-to.

The United States ambassador to France, Charles Kushner, the father of Mr. Trump’s son-in-law, Jared, has been twice summoned by the French government over comments he has made about French domestic affairs. The U.S. ambassador to Belgium was also summoned for comments he made.

Mr. Hoekstra also raised eyebrows when he invited the right-wing populist activist Tamara Lich, who had been convicted of organizing the trucker convoy that wreaked havoc in Ottawa for a month in 2022, to this year’s 4th of July party at the ambassador’s official residence.

Mr. Hoekstra has been accused of political interference in another nation’s domestic affairs. In 2020, while serving as U.S. ambassador to the Netherlands in the first Trump administration, he hosted an event at the U.S. embassy with a nativist, anti-immigrant Dutch party.

Expelling a U.S. ambassador would be a first for Canada, but far from unprecedented globally.

American ambassadors have been expelled during major geopolitical crises in the past, including during the Cold War, both World Wars, as well as more recently during crises with Latin American countries such as Venezuela.

Mr. Hoekstra’s stance in Canada aligns with the U.S. administration’s foreign policy elsewhere. The State Department has made significant efforts to cultivate and promote identarian politics in Europe through visits and senior official meetings with European political parties and other organizations sharing these ideas, including in Germany and Britain.

Representatives of the business community said Mr. Hoekstra had been a solid interlocutor during tumultuous times for the relationship between the two nations.

The U.S. Embassy in Canada recommended speaking to some business leaders about their working relationship with Mr. Hoekstra. They included Rick Tachuk, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada, a private, nonprofit membership organization promoting trade and investment across the border; and Beth Burke, chief executive of the Canadian American Business Council, a nonprofit, nonpartisan group.

Mr. Tachuk says that Mr. Hoekstra has been available to business leaders and cares about the U.S.-Canada trade relationship.

“He at times can be blunt, but, in many respects, that is an advantage for us because he helps articulate the view of the president, and helps us understand what the challenges are,” Mr. Tachuk said in an interview on Friday.

“Ambassador Hoekstra has to deliver some very unpopular messages here in Canada. It’s a tough job but he’s doing his best,” he added.

Ms. Burke said Mr. Hoekstra was well connected across the administration and an effective messenger.

“I also really value knowing where you stand in a situation. Sometimes pleasantries and diplomatic speak muddy the waters,” she added.

item.title: Syrian Convicted in Austria of Civil War Abuses Is Detained in Syria
item.description:
When a court in Vienna last month convicted two former Syrian officials of abuses during their country’s civil war, the case was celebrated as a groundbreaking pursuit of justice for victims of the fallen Syrian dictatorship.

But weeks later, one of those convicted, Musab Abu Rukbah, a former police chief, left Austria and traveled back to Syria after appealing his eight-year sentence. Now the Syrian government has announced that it has arrested him.

Syria’s Internal Security Forces said on Saturday that they had detained Mr. Abu Rukbah as part of “ongoing security operations to prosecute those involved in terrorism cases and take the necessary legal action against them.” The arrest came after reports that he had returned to his hometown, Nawa, in the southern province of Daraa.

Mr. Abu Rukbah, 54, had not been deemed a flight risk by a higher court in Vienna and was free while the appeal process was underway, Christina Salzborn, the vice president of the Regional Court of Vienna, said earlier this month.

Mr. Abu Rukbah had been released without conditions after a brief detention at the time of his indictment in January 2025, and he was not under any reporting requirements, travel ban or obligation to surrender his passport, Ms. Salzborn said.

But earlier this month, after Syrian activists posted on social media that they had learned of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s return, a lawyer representing victims in the case against him said she had applied for an international arrest warrant. The lawyer, Tatiana Urdaneta Wittek, is the director of the Center for the Enforcement of Human Rights International, a nonprofit organization in Vienna.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek said this month that Mr. Abu Rukbah’s return to Syria was grounds enough for an arrest warrant to be issued, though she also noted that Syria does not have an extradition treaty with Austria. A hearing date for Mr. Abu Rukbah’s appeal had not been set.

“With his escape to Syria, he is withdrawing from the proceedings before they are final,” Ms. Urdaneta Wittek said.

The court in Austria has made no public announcement about any warrant for Mr. Abu Rukbah’s arrest. Earlier this month, Roman Valach, a lawyer who represented Mr. Abu Rukbah at the trial, declined to comment on his whereabouts.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek and Mr. Valach could not immediately be reached for comment on Saturday after the announcement of Mr. Abu Rukbah’s arrest.

His return home is a test for Syria’s government, which is struggling to deliver justice for the hundreds of thousands of victims of the country’s civil war, 18 months after overthrowing the dictatorship of Bashar al-Assad.

Ms. Urdaneta Wittek’s application for a warrant, which was seen by The New York Times, said that an investigative group specializing in international justice cases, Arctic Wind Solutions, had confirmed with the Syrian border authorities that Mr. Abu Rukbah had crossed into Syria early on the morning of July 29.

Mr. Abu Rukbah’s apparent escape was an embarrassment for the Austrian authorities and a blow to his many victims after a 10-year investigation of him and a former intelligence official, Khaled al-Halabi.

Asyad Almousa, who was among those who testified against Mr. Abu Rukbah in Vienna, said before the announcement of his arrest that a whole new case now had to be built in Syria. “We are starting from zero,” he said, “which means years more of agonizing judicial process.”

Mr. Abu Rukbah and Mr. al-Halabi had claimed asylum in Austria after arriving in 2015, several years after the start of Syria’s civil war. They were convicted, in a rarity there, under the principle of universal jurisdiction, which allows a country to prosecute individuals for grave crimes committed elsewhere.

Twenty Syrian survivors testified against the two former officials during the trial, describing harrowing details of lasting physical and psychological trauma at their hands.

Mr. al-Halabi was convicted of torture and other crimes. Mr. Abu Rukbah was convicted on charges that included aggravated coercion and sexual coercion. Both men were sentenced to eight years in prison and lodged appeals through their lawyers.

“I feel a deep sadness seeing this happen,” said Mr. Almousa, the victim who had testified against Mr. Abu Rukbah. “Years of demanding our rights went into the wind because of the Austrian justice system’s carelessness. How was a man sentenced to eight years let go, free and not monitored?”

Naz Kucuktekin contributed reporting from Vienna.

]]>

item.title: Professor’s Death Leaves Behind Hard Questions for Cambridge on Race and Hiring
item.description:
When Cambridge University interviewed Jason Arday for one of the most prestigious sociology positions in the world, he was an early career scholar and underqualified, by the school’s own standards.

Cambridge’s requirements, reviewed by The New York Times, called for “an outstanding research record of international stature” and a “proven successful track record” supervising Ph.D. students. Dr. Arday had a modest publication record and had bounced from one university to the next — not staying long enough to oversee a full three-year-or-more doctorate.

Cambridge hired him anyway in 2023, making him, at 37, the university’s youngest Black professor at a time when the school was under pressure to diversify. In doing so, Cambridge thrust him into the international limelight, giving him a platform at one of the world’s elite universities to champion academic diversity and making him a target for critics.

Dr. Arday was found dead in London on Friday, days after resigning his job amid accusations that he had plagiarized chunks of his papers, embellished parts of his recently published memoir and fabricated aspects of his life story. The controversy exploded along cultural fault lines — race, neurodiversity and academic hiring.

In his Aug. 5 resignation later, he wrote, “I no longer wish to feel as though I am living under a constant spotlight, where every aspect of my life is subject to public examination and judgment.” He added, “This is not the end of my work. It is simply the end of this chapter.”

His family said that, since starting at Cambridge, Dr. Arday had faced a campaign of scrutiny intended to undermine him. That became too much for him, they said.

Questions about Dr. Arday’s career are unlikely to end with his death, however, because they were as much about Cambridge as they were as about him. The centuries-old alma mater of Isaac Newton, William Wordsworth and kings and queens, Cambridge now faces deep scrutiny about its decision-making, even from its own faculty.

While Dr. Arday was underqualified for his job, he had a remarkable story: a tale of being diagnosed early with autism and having such significant developmental delays that he spent his entire childhood in a special-needs school. In his account, he did not speak until age 11 or read until 18, yet he managed to earn his doctorate and begin giving keynote speeches on the academic circuit. Also, he had run 30 marathons in 35 days for charity, a feat that would have placed him among the world’s elite athletes.

If, in hindsight, elements of Dr. Arday’s story seemed too good to be true, Cambridge ignored repeated warning signs. A review of internal Cambridge documents and interviews with former colleagues and associates shows that, in addition to passing over more experienced candidates for the job, administrators gushed publicly about Dr. Arday’s scholarship and privately disregarded complaints about his work. They declined to investigate plagiarism concerns and accused his critics of a “vile campaign” to discredit him.

Dr. Arday’s claims about not speaking were false, a former classmate and a speech professional who worked with him told The New York Times. His supposedly remarkable trajectory from nonverbal preteen to Ph.D. had no precedent in medical literature, experts in developmental and speech delays say. That should have set off alarm bells for the Cambridge hiring committee, which included a child psychiatrist who had done research on autism, experts said.

Before Dr. Arday’s death, conservative commentators seized on his fall as evidence of diversity-and-inclusion efforts run amok. They said that Cambridge had been so eager to diversify that administrators let their judgment be clouded.

“They seem to have drunk the D.E.I. Kool-Aid,” Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former Conservative lawmaker in Britain, said early this week on The Telegraph’s “Daily T” podcast.

Prominent academics on the left agree that Cambridge must answer for its decisions. They say that the ordeal has fueled racism and cast unjustified aspersions on accomplished scholars of color.

Cambridge said on Friday that it was “desperately saddened” to hear of Dr. Arday’s death. An administrator, in a letter to the faculty on Tuesday, called the misconduct accusations “an aberration” and “troubling.” A spokesman separately declined to answer a list of questions about his hiring and his time there, citing a planned independent investigation — a difficult inquiry that will likely be made even more uncomfortable following Dr. Arday’s death.

Dr. Arday, for his part, had worked hard to silence any questioning of his credentials. When a journalist for Times Higher Education, a respected academic industry publication, asked about plagiarism last year, a prominent British defamation law firm helped kill the article, the journalist said. Dr. Arday later reported the journalist to the police.

When a scholar from another university questioned his work, Dr. Arday turned the tables and filed a racism complaint with the other school, according to someone with direct knowledge of the complaint. That person, like some others who spoke to The Times, spoke on the condition of anonymity to avoid being dragged publicly into the controversy.

Dr. Arday never squarely addressed the questions of plagiarism and fabrication.

But what is clear from interviews and public records is that elements of the story would have been easy for Cambridge to check.

Dr. Arday, the child of Ghanaian immigrants, grew up in public housing in an ethnically mixed, working-class quarter of South London. Early on, he was identified as having learning difficulties.

Dr. Arday has claimed that before age 11, he could understand language but not speak. In 2022, before interviewing with Cambridge, he said that he had been educated exclusively in a special-needs school “with other pupils that had very severe learning difficulties and physical disabilities.”

In his memoir, published on Tuesday, he gave a different account, saying he attended a mainstream school but spent time sequestered alone in a classroom, again without speaking.

Both tales are false, according to people who knew Dr. Arday as a child and spoke with The Times before his death.

A speech professional who worked closely with the young Dr. Arday recalled him having a language delay but speaking with both children and adults.

One former schoolmate, Jonathan Stewart, recalled Dr. Arday cracking jokes and putting on playful accents in a minivan on the way to church activities as children.

While nonverbal children can certainly learn to speak, even at a late age, the rapid development described by Dr. Arday has no precedent in clinical literature, three experts on autism and speech said.

“In over 40 years of practice and being very acquainted with literature, I’ve never heard of that happening,” said Stephen Camarata, a speech science expert with Vanderbilt Health’s Developmental Disabilities Lab. “It just stretches credulity.”

An established chair at Cambridge, a permanently funded position that comes with prestige and research support, is among the academic world’s most sought-after jobs.

Dr. Arday applied for an established chair of education at Jesus College, one of Cambridge’s oldest institutions, dating to the 15th century. The university advertised internationally for the job and convened a panel of nine experts to review the candidates.

The panel selected four finalists, inviting them to Cambridge for two days of interviews. Dr. Arday was up against three more senior scholars, including two women of color, according to a person familiar with the hiring process.

Dr. Arday’s published papers and his thesis had dozens of grammatical errors, along with identical quotes attributed to different people.

At Cambridge, the finalists were asked to submit just one piece of research, according to the person familiar with the process.

It is not clear which piece he submitted, or whether members of the hiring panel reviewed Dr. Arday’s speeches and interviews. If they had, they would have found elements of his story that stretched belief, like the marathon claim, or were demonstrably false, like his public assertion that he had been on the British television series “Seven Up.” (Dr. Arday’s spokesman recently said that the assertion should not have been taken literally.)

Experts said that Cambridge’s hiring panel was well equipped to question Dr. Arday’s very public claims about his childhood. Some committee members had published papers about teaching students with learning disabilities and about inclusion in education.

One influential member of the hiring panel, the child psychiatrist Paul Ramchandani, had published a paper on music therapy for children with autism. Given his expertise, he would have been in position to question Dr. Arday’s assertion that he learned to speak at 11 and read at 18, said Howard Shane, the director emeritus of the Center for Communication Enhancement at Boston Children’s Hospital.

“That should raise a red flag,” he said in an interview early this week. “There’s no question about that.”

Dr. Ramchandani and others on the panel did not respond to requests for comment.

The committee hired Dr. Arday, in a decision that the education department chair described at the time as unanimous. Cambridge’s lengthy hiring announcement highlighted his remarkable personal story, which garnered media coverage on both sides of the Atlantic.

Cambridge had so few Black professors that it was under pressure from faculty and students to diversify. It had set modest targets for increasing applications from people of color for academic posts.

On the BBC, the education department chair, Hilary Cremin, told Dr. Arday that he was “the best in the world in terms of the research you do.” She did not respond to requests for comment.

Three months after Dr. Arday’s hiring, two British scholars, Martyn Hammersley and David Harris, privately wrote to Cambridge, alerting administrators to potential plagiarism in one of Dr. Arday’s papers.

Dr. Cremin, the department chair, replied that she had met with Dr. Arday, and that he had agreed to address concerns in the paper. She also mentioned his “ongoing experiences of direct and indirect racism,” along with “significant health issues” that had affected his work on the paper in question, according to an email, which was first reported on a former professor’s newsletter and the academic integrity website Retraction Watch.

Dr. Harris, whose work has challenged whether racism is ingrained in society, responded by suggesting that Cambridge also review Dr. Arday’s other papers and his thesis. “Prof Arday badly needs critical friends, in my view, not sycophants,” he wrote.

He never got a reply, he said.

Nor did Cambridge act months later after journals appended corrections on two of Dr. Arday’s papers. Then, in September 2025, Times Higher Education sent Cambridge a dossier of more than 60 pages that detailed apparent plagiarism in Dr. Arday’s work.

A reporter and editor at the publication, Jack Grove, had enlisted experts to review Dr. Arday’s thesis.

One of them, David Sanders of Purdue University, told The Times that, going into the review, he knew nothing about Jason Arday. But when Dr. Sanders sat down to analyze the thesis, he concluded it was “extensively plagiarized.”

Cambridge continued to back its star professor, telling Mr. Grove that questions about Dr. Arday’s thesis would have to be addressed by the school that had awarded his doctorate, Liverpool John Moores University. Concerns about his research, Cambridge said, would similarly have to be handled by others. Liverpool John Moores stood by his doctorate.

At Cambridge, faculty members and allies hurriedly drafted a letter in anticipation of Mr. Grove’s article. “The integrity of higher education is at risk if we do not take a stand and speak out against the systematic attempts to erase Black scholarship,” they wrote in the letter, a copy of which was seen by The Times.

But Mr. Grove’s article never ran. Dr. Arday’s lawyers threatened legal action, and Times Higher Education spiked it. Dr. Arday also filed a police complaint against Mr. Grove, which led to a harassment investigation that was later dropped.

The plagiarism charges burst into public view last month when a former Cambridge scholar, Nathan Cofnas, wrote about them in his newsletter. Dr. Cofnas is known for his work suggesting that Black people were genetically predisposed to be less intelligent than white people. The university had cut ties with him in 2024.

Retraction Watch quickly expanded on Dr. Cofnas’s reporting. But once again, Cambridge defended Dr. Arday, saying he was “the victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility, which must stop,” according to an email seen by The Times.

After new questions surfaced, casting doubt on Dr. Arday’s story, he resigned. Cambridge’s tone shifted.

But the fallout from Cambridge’s enthusiastic promotion of Dr. Arday’s story could last for years. “This has really done some harm,” Dr. Camarata, the speech specialist, said before Dr. Arday’s death.

He said that over the years, he heard from families of children with severe autism hoping for a miracle. “I never want to take away anybody’s hope,” he said, “but this story really has created some unreasonable expectations and false hopes, and I hate that.”

Heidi Mirza, an emeritus professor of education at University College London who once mentored Dr. Arday, said in an interview this past week that he had been ill-served by university administrators’ carelessness in their efforts to demonstrate their commitment to diversity.

“He’s a pawn,” she said, “whose ambition made him vulnerable.”

Georgia Gee, Susan C. Beachy and Kitty Bennett contributed research.

item.title: After Women in India Joined Protests, Online Harassment Followed
item.description: Rhiya Ahir has suffered constant online abuse from trolls after an image of her at a protest in Mumbai last month went viral. ]]>
